source.title: SUA: Stealthy Multimodal Large Language Model Unlearning Attack
source.authors: Xianren Zhang; Hui Liu; Delvin Ce Zhang; Xian-Feng Tang; Qi He; Dongwon Lee; Su-Hang Wang

page_placements.theme: Uneven transfer of unlearning across modalities and languages

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether attacks recover knowledge after MLLM unlearning, using multimodal attack methods and prompt attacks in a new setting.
record.gate_note: The study tests paraphrasing and a jailbreak-style visual prompt, and reports results for its own universal image perturbation attack. The latter does not match the listed attack types in versions B–E, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. Related-work claims about other studies are not recorded as results. Secondary metrics and some baselines are omitted; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: It applies GD and NPO unlearning to two MLLMs on MLLMU-Bench and CLEAR. It then measures forget-set recovery under paraphrasing, FigStep, GCG text tokens and its own universal image perturbation (SUA). This is a new, multimodal setting for the claim. The paraphrase, FigStep and GCG results bear on A and E. SUA, a white-box optimized image perturbation, fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that unlearned MLLMs hide rather than erase knowledge, since SUA recovers it across datasets, methods, models and defenses and generalizes to unseen samples. They also report that baseline attacks (paraphrase, random noise, FigStep) do not significantly increase recovery, and that SUA works in a grey-box setting.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses GD and NPO to unlearn MLLMs, then trains universal image perturbations (and, in an additional experiment, GCG textual tokens) as attacks. It does not reproduce the cited LLM unlearning recovery procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by dataset, unlearning method, model, defense condition, and attack type. The study reports a detection defense and a denoising defense; SUA remains effective under both.

fits_no_version.finding: A white-box universal image perturbation (SUA) raises forget accuracy from 3.67 to 20.67 (original 56) and factuality from 0.56 to 2.05 (original 2.62). It works across NPO, Idefics2 and both defenses, and on unseen samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized adversarial input perturbations in a non-text modality recover unlearned MLLM knowledge that prompt attacks do not.

fits_no_version.finding: A joint image-perturbation plus GCG attack (SUA+) gives 21.33% accuracy and 2.20 factuality.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Joint visual and textual optimized attacks recover more than either alone.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results. Chance accuracy is not stated. The retain-set comparison does not include the original model, and the text reports limited model coverage: two MLLMs and fictional-profile datasets. The study does not test quantization or internal activation edits.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional metric values, including ROUGE-L and BLEU, and further attack-baseline results for random noise and nucleus sampling in Tables 1–5 and 7–8. They are omitted to prioritize unlearned references, prompt-only attacks, and SUA results on the main accuracy/factuality measures. The retained-set factuality, ROUGE-L, and BLEU values in Table 6 are also omitted.

untested.parts: Retain-set utility relative to the original model; chance level is not stated.
No activation ablation or internal analysis.
Other languages and in-context information are not tested.
No new robust unlearning method is tested.

missing.what: Grey-box SUA results (e.g. 7.83% accuracy and 1.24 factuality on GD MLLMU-Bench), not recorded and not declared in rows_left_out
Few-shot perturbation training: 1-10 samples suffice for effective SUA

record.verdict_notes: Versions were relabelled from V1/V5 to A/E. Factuality is judged by GPT-4o, and the paraphrase and sampling baselines use best-of-6 selection. No uncertainty estimates are reported. All data are fictitious profiles. The supports label for A covers only simple attacks. The paper's main result (SUA) argues against unlearning being deletion, but an optimized white-box image perturbation is neither a 'simple attack' nor prompting, so it sits under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports forget-set performance and retain-set performance, but does not state a chance level or compare retain-set utility with the original model.
No fine-tuning of the unlearned model on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten knowledge is tested.
No activation direction is ablated and no internal analysis establishes deletion versus blocked access.
Tests paraphrasing, FigStep, and optimized textual tokens; does not test other languages or in-context information.
No newer unlearning method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.

source_check.notes: Paraphrase and sampling take the best of 6 responses, and no uncertainty is reported. Idefics2 unlearning method is not stated. SUA rows (the headline 3.67 to 20.67) are linked to no version, while the white-box GCG text-token rows are linked to E, so the main finding is in no verdict. Undefended GD paraphrase/FigStep rows are absent on the authors' words. NPO and defended rows with similar or smaller gains are partial because the authors do not comment on them.

statements.correction: GD on LLaVA-1.5-7B, MLLMU-Bench: forget accuracy 56.00 to 3.67; paraphrase 4.67, FigStep 5.83 (authors: not significant). The study's own white-box universal image perturbation reaches 20.67.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers or findings for this study, only its cited rows (r1, r2). Those rows do support A.
